title: Frank Falls Out the Window

jokes.text: Frank hanging his ass out the window to fart, negotiating re-entry with Charlie
jokes.setup: Charlie asks if Frank is done farting before letting him back in
jokes.punchline: Frank flatly says 'No' — he is not done, and continues to hang out the window
jokes.explanation: Perfect cold open energy. The image of Frank dangling his ass out a window is visually absurd, but the flat 'No' delivery is what makes it land. Character-specific — only Frank would do this without shame. Sets the squalor tone immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: makes Frank hang his ass out the window for farting from eating rum ham on a Grilled Charlie

jokes.text: Charlie explains the 'Grilled Charlie' with rum ham caused the farting, then Frank demands another one anyway
jokes.setup: Charlie diagnoses the problem: a Grilled Charlie topped with rum ham is 'a stomach bomb, too much for your system'
jokes.punchline: Frank's response: 'Then make me another one. If I'm gonna stick my ass out the window, I'm gonna eat.'
jokes.explanation: This is exceptionally character-integrated. Frank's logic — 'since I'm already suffering the consequence, I might as well keep causing it' — is perversely airtight and completely Frank. 'Grilled Charlie' and 'rum ham' are dense lore callbacks, the economy is superb, and the line is instantly quotable. Among the best jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: 'If I'm gonna stick my ass out the window, I'm gonna eat.'

jokes.text: Frank falls out the window mid-sentence while Charlie is lecturing him
jokes.setup: Charlie is mid-rant about Frank's stomach: 'I feel like it's gonna be a week before your system gets back to normal. You can't just eat whatever you...'
jokes.punchline: Frank screams 'Charlie...!' followed by crashing and shattering sounds — he has fallen out the window
jokes.explanation: The mid-lecture cutoff is structurally clean — Charlie's responsible-adult mode is shattered (literally) at exactly the right moment. The setup pays off the whole cold open's premise. High structural economy because the entire cold open built to this.

jokes.text: Mac arguing he was 'the first one' to come up with the chicken/steak contamination plan, interrupting something important
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are having a seemingly important conversation; Mac keeps insisting he originated an idea
jokes.punchline: Dennis flatly denies it; Mac's desperate need for credit over a scheme involving contaminating steaks with chickens is treated as a weighty grievance
jokes.explanation: Mac's pathological need for recognition is well-established character comedy, but the specific bit (credit for chicken/steak contamination) is thin. Works as texture but doesn't land as a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Your mother's dead

jokes.text: Frank interrupts with 'Your mother's dead' as an offhand conversation-stopper
jokes.setup: Frank barges in mid-argument and blurts 'Your mother's dead' as if dropping a bomb
jokes.punchline: Dennis and Dee respond 'Yeah, we know she's dead' — completely unfazed, treating it as old news
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Frank thinks he's delivering devastating news, and the kids treat it like a minor inconvenience. The casual 'yeah we know' response is the real punchline, suggesting their family dysfunction runs so deep that their mother's death is basically a footnote.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I was just kidding. Your mother's not really dead. I dropped that bomb to soften the blow. We're getting divorced.

jokes.text: Frank follows 'Your mother's dead' with 'I was just kidding — your mother's not really dead. I dropped that bomb to soften the blow' for 'We're getting divorced'
jokes.setup: Frank backtracks on the death announcement as a joke, claiming it was strategic: a fake death to soften the real news
jokes.punchline: 'I dropped that bomb to soften the blow' — the 'real' news is a divorce, which Frank considers worse than death
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely clever structural joke. The 'I was just kidding' reversal is the first surprise, but the REAL punchline is the implicit claim that a divorce is worse news than a death — delivered with complete Frank sincerity. Tight two-beat structure, excellent misdirection, highly quotable logic. One of the episode's best constructed jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You're not a funny guy. Don't do bits. They never play.

jokes.text: Dennis tells Frank 'You're not a funny guy. Don't do bits. They never play.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just done a genuinely funny bit (fake death as softener) that everyone dismissed
jokes.punchline: Dennis's confident, authoritative dismissal — 'they never play' — is itself a bit, delivered by a man who just watched a funny bit play
jokes.explanation: Dennis's condescension is a consistent character trait and it works here. There's also a meta-layer since the bit DID play. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, I see skull!

jokes.text: Post-fall Frank doesn't recognize anyone and says 'And who might you be?' to people he's known for years
jokes.setup: Everyone rushes to check on Frank after his fall; they expect him to be injured but okay
jokes.punchline: Frank looks at his closest associates and politely asks 'And who might you be?' as if meeting strangers
jokes.explanation: Classic amnesia setup, well-executed as a plot reveal. The formal 'And who might you be?' is a nice touch — very unlike Frank's usual vulgarity — signaling the personality shift. Functional but not inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What day is it?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It's Thursday.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, it's Friday.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's Friday.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Did I lose a day?

jokes.text: Mac: 'Uh-oh, he's finally lost it. Should we toss him in a home?' Dee: 'Yep, I'll get the car.'
jokes.setup: Frank appears confused after his fall; everyone is alarmed
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dee's instant, clinical response is to send him to a nursing home with no emotional hesitation whatsoever
jokes.explanation: The speed and practicality of Dee volunteering to 'get the car' is the joke. These people have zero sentimentality. Good character economy — expresses the gang's essential awfulness in two lines.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What is the capital of Pennsylvania?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Philadelphia.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Is it Pittsburgh?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: At one point, it was Philly.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I don't think they change it, Charlie.

jokes.text: Charlie shows Frank's exposed skull wound and says 'Oh, I see skull!'
jokes.setup: Frank insists his head is fine after the fall; Charlie points out evidence to the contrary
jokes.punchline: Mac gasps 'That's horrific!' while Charlie simply announces 'Oh, I see skull!' — a completely unfiltered, childlike observation of a gruesome injury
jokes.explanation: Charlie's matter-of-fact 'Oh, I see skull!' is a great line — the casual wonder in it is very Charlie. Highly quotable within the show's fanbase. The contrast with Mac's horrified gasp is effective.

dialogue.line: Who's the President?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: George Bush.
Nah, I was just kidding. The real president is Dick Cheney. He's pulling all the strings.

jokes.text: The gang tests Frank's mental state: 'What day is it?' — Frank says Wednesday, Charlie says wrong it's Tuesday, then someone confirms it IS Wednesday
jokes.setup: The gang tries to test Frank's cognition with simple questions
jokes.punchline: The 'tester' doesn't even know what day it is — Charlie confidently corrects Frank, then has to admit Charlie was right all along
jokes.explanation: Smart reversal — the person administering the sanity test fails it themselves. Reinforces that the gang is barely more functional than brain-damaged Frank. Good structural economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Charlie's theory that Frank went through a time portal window to 2006

jokes.text: Capital of Pennsylvania test: Frank says 'Philadelphia'; Charlie agrees; Dennis corrects them both — it's not Philadelphia
jokes.setup: Mac suggests an easier question: 'What is the capital of Pennsylvania?'
jokes.punchline: Frank says Philadelphia; Charlie agrees 'at one point it was Philly, I'm pretty sure'; Dennis has to point out you don't change capitals
jokes.explanation: Charlie's confident but wrong 'at one point it was Philly, I'm pretty sure' is perfectly Charlie — genuine conviction in total ignorance. The escalating wrongness of the testers undermines the whole sanity test, which is the meta-joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac and Dennis
dialogue.line: No, they haven't. No, they haven't.

jokes.text: Frank's presidential answer: 'George Bush'... then corrects himself: 'The real president is Dick Cheney. He's pulling all the strings.'
jokes.setup: Mac asks who the President of the United States is — the easiest possible sanity check question
jokes.punchline: Frank says 'George Bush' (plausible for 2006), then self-corrects to Dick Cheney as the shadow president 'pulling all the strings'
jokes.explanation: Two-beat structure is perfect: the initial answer (George Bush) seems to pass the test, then the correction to Cheney reframes it as a conspiratorial Frank worldview that's both wrong AND coherent for his character. 'He's pulling all the strings' is delivered with absolute conviction — peak Frank paranoia. Highly quotable and exceptionally character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We can't repeat the same mistakes of the past. Keep Charlie away from Frank. He's drawn to him for some inexplicable reason.

jokes.text: Charlie's theory: 'What happened is he went through the window, and the window seemed to be some sort of portal to the year 2006'
jokes.setup: Everyone is trying to explain Frank's confused mental state; Dennis offers the rational explanation (concussion)
jokes.punchline: Charlie proposes that the window is literally a time portal to 2006, which he states as a reasonable hypothesis
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Charlie logic — presented with total sincerity in the face of an obvious explanation. The specificity ('portal to the year 2006' rather than just 'the past') is what elevates it. Character integration is near-perfect; only Charlie believes this. Sets up the episode's running gag engine.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Dee suggests Wyclef Jean charity scam, then sings 'Gone Till November' incorrectly

jokes.text: Dennis: 'It's crazy, but stranger things have happened.' Mac and Charlie: 'No, they haven't. No, they haven't.'
jokes.setup: Dennis halfheartedly entertains the time portal theory
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie's synchronized, emphatic rejection: 'No, they haven't. No, they haven't.' — the two characters most prone to absurd logic are suddenly the voice of reason
jokes.explanation: The doubled denial ('No they haven't, no they haven't') has a nice comic rhythm. The irony that Mac and Charlie of all people are shutting down an absurd theory is a good character-reversal joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: How do you not have fish?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Two can play at that game. Banging your sister is perverted.

jokes.text: Dee immediately guesses the plan: 'Are you talking about taking all his money and kicking him out?'
jokes.setup: Dennis is building toward revealing a scheme; there's a brief pause
jokes.punchline: Dee cuts straight to the mercenary heart of it without any prompting — 'Of course that's what I'm talking about'
jokes.explanation: Good character shorthand — these people are so transparently awful that even the reveal of a scheme is predictable to them. Dee's instant read is funny and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm working toward becoming a veterinarian

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I have Broadway dreams

jokes.text: Dennis breaks into 'Gone Till November' — doesn't know the words, trails off into mumbling
jokes.setup: Dennis's scheme involves the Wyclef Jean charity angle, so he starts singing the Wyclef song
jokes.punchline: He confidently begins but quickly devolves into mumbling because he doesn't know the lyrics — 'You don't know the song' / 'I didn't know the song. There was a good bounce to it.'
jokes.explanation: 'There was a good bounce to it' as a defense for launching into a song you don't know the words to is a perfect Dennis rationalization. The visual of him trailing off mid-lyric adds to it. His complete lack of self-awareness is in full display.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You're what, 25, 26?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah.

jokes.text: Restaurant scene: 'Fresh fish daily' / 'How do you not have fish?'
jokes.setup: Frank reads 'Fresh fish daily' off the menu or signage at the restaurant
jokes.punchline: Immediately: 'How do you not have fish?' — the restaurant advertising fresh fish daily has no fish
jokes.explanation: Quick, functional restaurant gag. Not especially original but executed with good economy. The briefness is its strength.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: There was a disaster in Haiti?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I invented the phone.

jokes.text: 'Two can play at that game. Banging your sister is perverted.'
jokes.setup: Frank appears to be responding to something said or implied at the table (possibly in response to a slight from the waiter)
jokes.punchline: Frank retorts with 'banging your sister is perverted' — a non sequitur accusation that escalates the conflict to an absurd place
jokes.explanation: The randomness is very Frank — he escalates to incest accusations over restaurant service. The specificity of 'banging your sister' over some other insult is what gives it character flavor. Somewhat disconnected without full visual context.

jokes.text: Frank tells Dennis and Dee they're 'what, 25, 26?' and not to worry, they have time — they're clearly middle-aged
jokes.setup: Frank, thinking it's 2006, is being encouraging about their careers — they're 'young' in his mind
jokes.punchline: He guesses they're 25–26 and assures them they have time before they 'move on' from their dreams — when they're obviously in their late 30s
jokes.explanation: Good layered joke — the audience knows these characters' ages and failed career arcs, so Frank's sincere encouragement lands as an indictment. Dennis and Dee's suppressed discomfort is implied. Character-specific pain for a show that rarely allows earnest emotion.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: This time, you and I are gonna be the ones that bang the strippers.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Why do you want to bang them?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Cause it's 2006, and you're still into women.

jokes.text: Frank: 'You don't want to be almost 40 working at a bar.' Dennis and Dee visible reaction.
jokes.setup: Frank is offering paternal wisdom about not letting too much time pass on dreams
jokes.punchline: He lands on 'you don't want to be almost 40 working at a bar' — which is EXACTLY what Dennis and Dee are
jokes.explanation: The accidental precision of Frank's warning is a sharp joke. Because he thinks it's 2006, his cautionary 'don't become X' perfectly describes what they already are. Dennis and Dee's silent reaction — enduring the accurate insult while pretending to be young professionals — is rich cringe territory. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: shows Frank his toe knife and explains using it to dig scum out of his toes

jokes.text: Frank: 'I know I've been a lousy dad, but there's only one person to blame for that: your whore mother.'
jokes.setup: Frank is having a rare moment of paternal self-reflection, seemingly about to take responsibility
jokes.punchline: The expected accountability pivot is immediately redirected: 'there's only one person to blame — your whore mother'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The setup mimics a sitcom redemption beat — 'I know I've been a lousy dad, but...' — and then Frank turns it completely inside out by blaming his dead ex-wife. Perfect misdirection, peak Frank character, highly quotable. The structure (self-awareness to deflection) is a classic Frank move executed flawlessly.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Botched toe!

jokes.text: Dennis and Dee scrambling to agree that giving all Frank's money to charity is a 'great idea' while barely concealing the grift
jokes.setup: Frank announces he wants to give away his money to charity; Dennis and Dee are trying to steer this money toward themselves
jokes.punchline: Their overwrought enthusiasm — 'Oh my gosh, no, we are super into helping people in need and poor people...' — is transparently fake
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — the insincerity is obvious and that's the joke. Doesn't add much beyond illustrating what we already know about these characters.

dialogue.speaker: Stripper
dialogue.line: Botched toe! Frank, that is disgusting!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Toe knife. Maybe I ought to try that.

jokes.text: Dee accidentally references the Haiti earthquake disaster to Frank who is in 2006 and it hasn't happened yet
jokes.setup: Dee mentions the Haiti charity they work with, referencing the 'Haiti disaster'
jokes.punchline: Frank asks 'There was a disaster in Haiti?' — it's 2006 in his mind; the earthquake was 2010. Dee scrambles
jokes.explanation: Smart use of the time-displacement premise. Dee's fumble (forgetting Frank doesn't know the future) is both a character mistake and a logical consequence of the episode's setup. The scrambling that follows is good sustained cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: He is on a bang path straight to the waitress.

jokes.text: Dennis claims to have invented the smartphone: 'That's because... I invented it.'
jokes.setup: Frank is amazed by Dennis's smartphone, having never seen one (it's '2006' in his mind)
jokes.punchline: Without missing a beat, Dennis claims he invented it
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dennis moment — his narcissism is so reflexive that when given an unexpected opening to claim genius, he takes it instantly. The speed of the reply ('That's because... I invented it') and his complete conviction make this. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's done. You were too old in 2006. You're way too old now. And you're bad at it.

jokes.text: Dee immediately claims she invented it too — then Dennis claims he invented it first and she 'copied him' — then Dee says she 'upgraded it'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just claimed to have invented the smartphone
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately also claims credit; they begin competing over who invented the phone first, with Dennis saying she copied him and Dee countering she 'upgraded it'
jokes.explanation: The escalation of competing invention claims is a good bit — mirrors the show's opening argument about the chicken scheme. The 'I upgraded it' is a nice touch, implying Dee is now the better inventor. Frank accepting all of this is the capper.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I feel like the only reason you wanted to be a vet was to keep the skins.

jokes.text: Frank: '(laughing) Oh, Dee, you bitch.' — warmly, as a term of endearment
jokes.setup: The family is sharing a warm toast after Frank expresses pride in his kids
jokes.punchline: Frank's laugh of genuine affection ends with 'Oh, Dee, you bitch' — the slur delivered as a loving nickname
jokes.explanation: The pivot from genuine warmth to casual vulgarity in a single breath is Frank's character in miniature. It's a small moment but perfectly executed. The word 'bitch' said in a tone of pure paternal pride is the whole joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You want to keep the skins, don't you?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: There's no denying the skins are fascinating.

jokes.text: Mac reveals the 2006 strip club plan — 'we brought home two strippers, so...' / 'Yeah, but he banged both of them'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to show Charlie what life could be like without Frank by recreating what they originally did in 2006
jokes.punchline: The original plan already failed spectacularly — Frank slept with both strippers — which makes the 'lesson' moot
jokes.explanation: Good contextual joke that uses the audience's understanding of past Frank behavior. The deflation of Mac's plan before it even starts is effective but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You're going bald and you have back fat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I am not going bald, and I do not have back fat.

jokes.text: Mac to Charlie at the strip club: ''Cause it's 2006 and you're still into women. Crazy.'
jokes.setup: Mac explains why he wants to bang the strippers, adding 'it's 2006 and you're still into women'
jokes.punchline: The implication — that Charlie's heterosexuality is a past-tense thing — reveals Mac knows something about Charlie (or himself) that he's dancing around; 'Crazy' adds the wink
jokes.explanation: This is a sharply-constructed joke about Mac's sexuality — a long-running character arc that pays off repeatedly. The 'it's 2006 and you're still into women' implies that in the present, something changed, but which 'something' is left gloriously ambiguous (Charlie's sexuality vs. Mac's own). 'Crazy' as the deadpan capper earns the laugh. High character integration, great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Also you're going bald.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm going bald?! Where in the hell am I possibly going bald?!

jokes.text: Mac's 'You haven't become... Just drop it, just drop it, just drop it.'
jokes.setup: Mac starts to say something revealing about Charlie's sexuality — 'you haven't become...'
jokes.punchline: He immediately pulls back — 'just drop it, just drop it, just drop it' — panic-walking away from something he was about to say about himself as much as Charlie
jokes.explanation: The abrupt self-cancellation is rich with Mac's deeply suppressed sexuality as a running character thread. The triple 'just drop it' is the desperate overcorrection of someone who knows exactly what they almost said. Excellent character integration — this only works with Mac in this context.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: There's no reason why a bald man who enjoys skins who has extra something-something around his belly can't be a goddamn veterinarian!

jokes.text: Frank shows up at the strip club with a visibly infected head wound; stripper offers to give him a lap dance 'maybe to make you feel better'
jokes.setup: Frank appears at the strip club with what Charlie described earlier as exposed skull; a stripper notices the horrific infection
jokes.punchline: The stripper's sympathy response is to offer a lap dance — implying this is somehow medically appropriate or just what strippers do
jokes.explanation: The lap dance as medical comfort is a funny bit of absurdist logic. Mostly works as a visual gag — the juxtaposition of grotesque wound and strip club setting — but the written joke is fairly thin.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I see fat spilling over the back of your pants on a pretty regular basis

jokes.text: Charlie's apartment reveal: booze hidden under the pillow, a steak knife in the bed
jokes.setup: Frank and a stripper are taken back to Charlie's apartment; Frank asks for booze
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately says 'Oh yeah, yeah — in the bed, under the pillow' — indicating hidden-liquor-in-bed is a normal and known system
jokes.explanation: The casual normality of booze stored under the pillow is good Charlie character detail. The steak knife discovery builds this into a revealing portrait of Charlie's living conditions. Character-specific visual comedy.

dialogue.line: Dennis and Dee wake up with a crack pipe, having smoked crack despite trying to stay clean

jokes.text: Charlie's 'toe knife' — a steak knife used to 'dig the scum out of my toes and cut my nails off'
jokes.setup: Mac's girlfriend/the stripper finds a steak knife in Charlie's bed and is alarmed
jokes.punchline: Charlie explains it's his 'toe knife' — specifically for pedicure-style scum removal and nail cutting — delivered as though this is completely normal
jokes.explanation: The 'toe knife' is a great piece of Charlie mythology. The word 'toe knife' itself is funny — 'toe' as an adjective applied to 'knife' creates a specific, revolting image. Charlie's added justification ('cleaner cut, really') pushes it into genius territory. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We'll get back on crack. I mean, on track. Unless you have more crack.

jokes.text: Frank echoing 'Toe knife. Maybe I ought to try that.'
jokes.setup: Everyone reacts in disgust to Charlie's toe knife explanation
jokes.punchline: Frank, fresh off a head injury and operating in 2006, considers adopting the toe knife as a practice
jokes.explanation: Good callback that uses Frank as a mirror for Charlie's lifestyle. Frank's immediate enthusiasm ('maybe I ought to try that') implies this is the kind of squalid innovation that appeals to him, which is true to character and feeds into the broader theme of Frank being drawn back to degeneracy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: No one in the history of crack has ever woken up in the morning with more crack.

jokes.text: Mac warns Charlie: Frank is on 'a bang path straight to the waitress'
jokes.setup: Mac pulls Charlie outside, concerned about where the night with Frank and strippers is heading
jokes.punchline: 'He is on a bang path straight to the waitress' — a very specific and bizarre concern that implies a known historical pattern
jokes.explanation: 'Bang path' as a noun/phrase is inventive. The idea that Frank has a predictable escalating sexual trajectory that ends specifically at the waitress is a very specific piece of show mythology. Charlie's immediate 'Oh shit, definitely want to avoid that' sells it. Highly quotable, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm a recovering crackhead, and this is my donkey-brained sister that I take care of.

jokes.text: Mac: 'He locked us out.' Charlie: 'He did?' Mac: 'Yes.' Charlie: 'So it is 2006.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie try to pull Frank out of the apartment but find themselves locked out
jokes.punchline: Charlie interprets being locked out as confirmation that the window is a time portal — 'So it is 2006' — presented as logical deduction
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie logic. The setup is two straight lines ('He locked us out.' / 'He did?') and the punchline ('So it is 2006') is completely non-sequitur but totally coherent within Charlie's worldview. The economy is near-perfect — nothing wasted. Among the best jokes in the episode. The triple exchange rhythm is flawless.

dialogue.line: Forged document where they crossed out 'Frank' and wrote 'Dee' and crossed out 'not' from 'not donkey brained'

jokes.text: Dennis's aside: 'Say what you want about Wyclef — he may have stolen money from his own people, but that man can write a goddamn song.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee are waiting and the Wyclef song plays; Dennis is in a reflective mood
jokes.punchline: Dennis offers a full moral audit of Wyclef — acknowledges the charity fraud against 'his own people' — but concludes the songwriting redeems him. Delivered with absolute sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The 'say what you want about X' construction is a classic dark-comedy formula, but the specific content — praising someone who defrauded earthquake victims because the songs are good — is particularly nihilistic. Dennis's sincerity is key. Good economy and genuine wit.

dialogue.speaker: Welfare Worker
dialogue.line: I'm done with this bullshit

jokes.text: Dennis delivers brutal honesty to Dee: 'The acting thing. It's done. But it's been done for a long time. I mean, you were too old in 2006. You're way too old now. And you're bad at it.'
jokes.setup: Dennis claims he wants to 'get real' with Dee about their futures, framing it as a gift of honesty
jokes.punchline: His verdict on her acting career: she was already too old in 2006, she's way too old now, and she's also just bad at it. Three separate brutal conclusions delivered as caring advice.
jokes.explanation: The three-point escalation — too old in 2006, way too old now, AND bad at it — is excellently structured. Each element is its own wound. The framing as 'getting real' and Dee's initial grateful response ('Thank you. For your honesty.') before it fully lands is excellent cringe setup. Dennis's oblivious sincerity in delivering the insults as kindness is pitch-perfect character work.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Obama just gives you the money; it's great.

jokes.text: Dee retaliates: 'The only reason you wanted to be a vet was to keep the skins.' — 'There's no denying the skins are fascinating.'
jokes.setup: Dee turns the honesty around on Dennis and his veterinarian dream
jokes.punchline: She claims he only wants to be a vet for the animal skins — which Dennis doesn't deny, instead confirming 'the skin of any animal is the most fascinating part'
jokes.explanation: Dennis's creepy fascination with skins is deeply character-specific and touches on his serial-killer-adjacent psychological profile that runs through the show. The fact that he doesn't deny it but doubles down ('the skin of any animal is the most fascinating part') is the best part — it makes the insult more damning by his own confirmation. Highly quotable and rewatchable.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: All the gang ending up at the welfare store, Charlie still insisting it's 2006

jokes.text: Dee tells Dennis he's going bald; Dennis explodes: 'I'm going bald?! What are you talking about?! Where in the hell am I possibly going bald?!'
jokes.setup: Dee follows up the skin comment with a secondary honesty bomb: 'Also, you're going bald'
jokes.punchline: Dennis, who has been completely composed delivering brutal truths to Dee, completely loses his composure over the baldness accusation — an asymmetric breakdown
jokes.explanation: Dennis's vanity is a core character trait and his disproportionate reaction to the baldness claim (versus his own brutality about Dee's career) is a great reveal of hypocrisy. The escalating denial and demand for mirrors is good physical cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Dennis's response to 'you want to keep the skins': 'There's no denying the skins are fascinating. It's the most fascinating part of the animal. The skin of any animal is the most fascinating part, but that's not why I wanted to become...'
jokes.setup: Dee has accused Dennis of pursuing veterinary school to collect animal skins
jokes.punchline: Dennis's rebuttal is not 'that's crazy' — it's a passionate defense of skins as objectively fascinating, before he remembers he was supposed to be denying the accusation
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. Dennis doesn't say 'I don't want to keep the skins' — he says 'you can't deny skins are fascinating' and delivers a lecture on WHY skins are fascinating before catching himself. This is a perfect piece of character writing: Dennis Reynolds accidentally confirming he is a potential serial killer while trying to defend himself. The comedic structure is impeccable — the audience is waiting for the denial and gets a passionate endorsement instead. This is the kind of joke that becomes a show touchstone.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: Mr. Doran? He passed away.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Frank laughing and calling for Jerry to stop the bit

jokes.text: Dee: 'I see fat spilling over the back of your pants on a pretty regular basis.' Dennis: '(stammers) What the hell are you talking about?!'
jokes.setup: In the spirit of mutual honesty, Dee continues piling on while Dennis is still processing the baldness claim
jokes.punchline: The 'fat spilling over the back of your pants' detail is specific and visually gross — and Dennis's incoherent stammer indicates it has landed
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe escalation. Specific visual detail ('back of your pants') works better than generic fat joke. Part of a well-constructed mutual-destruction sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You goddamn bitch! You wouldn't know a good idea if it smacked you in a tit!

jokes.text: Dee's secondary attack: 'Also you're going bald.' — mid-argument, completely unprompted
jokes.setup: The siblings are exchanging devastating personal attacks
jokes.punchline: Dee drops 'also you're going bald' as a separate item, presented as an additional data point in an ongoing argument rather than an insult
jokes.explanation: Good escalation beat. The 'also' framing is perfect — it's added to the list of grievances like it's another item in a formal complaint. Dennis's explosive reaction and Dee's offer to get two mirrors is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You goddamn bitch! You wouldn't know a good idea if it smacked you in a tit!

jokes.text: Dennis: 'There's no reason why a bald man who enjoys skins who has a little bit of extra something-something around his belly can't be a goddamn veterinarian!'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee have been trading insults; Dennis is trying to pivot back to being supportive
jokes.punchline: In attempting to give Dee encouragement, Dennis accidentally catalogs all his own deficiencies ('bald man who enjoys skins with extra something-something') in a single breath — confirming everything Dee said
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliantly constructed callback that ties together three separate insults into one self-incriminating speech. The phrase 'extra something-something' as a euphemism for his own fat is both a denial and a confirmation. The speech is inadvertently a self-portrait of everything he denied. One of the episode's best jokes structurally. 'A bald man who enjoys skins' is an exceptional phrase.

dialogue.line: Frank writes them a check but it's dated 2006, making it invalid

jokes.text: Dee: 'You are a wrinkled bitch!'
jokes.setup: The mutual honesty session has completely devolved; Dee is now responding to Dennis's 'extra something-something' quasi-support
jokes.punchline: 'You are a wrinkled bitch!' — Dee drops the pretense entirely and goes full insult
jokes.explanation: Pure id. 'Wrinkled bitch' is a funny specific insult — 'wrinkled' as an adjective doing specific work rather than a generic epithet. Momentum of the scene carries it more than craft.

dialogue.line: Charlie's roommate interviews including cat food questions and Frank saying he'd always eat it

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I'm gonna tell you something, my characters are good.'
jokes.setup: Dee has insulted Dennis and they're escalating; Dennis circles back to defending his acting ability (which was not under discussion — Dee's was)
jokes.punchline: Dennis randomly asserts the quality of his acting characters in a moment of pure ego-defense irrelevance
jokes.explanation: Dennis's random need to defend his unthreatened acting career while attacking Dee's is a perfect character moment. The non sequitur nature of 'my characters are good' in this context is the joke — he can't even let Dee's failures be about Dee without inserting his own imagined superiority.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Charlie trying to throw the waitress out the window to send her back to 2006

jokes.text: Morning after: a crack pipe visible on the table; Dennis and Dee discover they've smoked crack
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee wake up disheveled in a morning-after scene after their touching reconciliation dinner
jokes.punchline: Their 'new beginnings' evening apparently ended with them buying and smoking crack cocaine — the crack pipe on the table is the visual punchline
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural beat — the warm 'to new beginnings' toast is immediately answered by a crack-morning hangover. Callbacks Dennis and Dee's history (they were crackheads in an early episode). The juxtaposition of their aspirational evening against the crack pipe is structurally excellent and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: We having a gang bang?

jokes.text: Dee: 'Well, it looks like we drank everything in the entire world, and then we went out and bought some crack, and we smoked it.'
jokes.setup: Dennis asks 'How'd this happen again?'
jokes.punchline: Dee's matter-of-fact recounting of the night's events — 'everything in the entire world' as a quantity of alcohol, followed by the completely casual crack purchase — is delivered with zero drama
jokes.explanation: 'We drank everything in the entire world' is a great hyperbolic deadpan phrase. The matter-of-fact pivot to 'and then we went out and bought some crack' treats the acquisition of crack cocaine as a mundane logistical step. Well-constructed and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Bank Teller
dialogue.line: can't cash the check because it's dated 2006

jokes.text: Dee: 'No one in the history of crack has ever woken up in the morning with more crack.'
jokes.setup: Dennis asks if Dee has more crack; Dee says no
jokes.punchline: Dee contextualizes the no: 'No one in the history of crack has ever woken up in the morning with more crack' — presenting it as a universal truth
jokes.explanation: This is a legitimately great line. The historical/universal framing ('no one in the history of crack') is perfectly constructed — it sounds like a confident pronouncement on human nature but is about drug logistics. Delivered deadpan by Dee, it's both funny and philosophically accurate about addiction. Highly quotable and among the best-crafted jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'we'll... pull ourselves together, and we'll... get back on crack. I mean, on track.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is reassuring Dee that the crack incident isn't a big deal
jokes.punchline: He accidentally says 'get back on crack' instead of 'on track' — then corrects himself while immediately asking if Dee has more crack
jokes.explanation: The Freudian slip is well-executed, and the immediate follow-up ('unless you have more crack') makes it land harder. The correction-then-reversal structure is classic. Dennis's inability to maintain the pretense of recovery even for one sentence is a great character beat.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'If I'm being very, very real, I need to be high on crack cocaine right now.'
jokes.setup: In the spirit of their new 'getting real' pact, Dennis applies the honesty framework to his crack craving
jokes.punchline: He invokes their dinner-table language ('being very, very real') specifically to admit he desperately needs more crack
jokes.explanation: Superb callback. The 'getting real' framing from the elegant dinner is now applied to 'I need crack right now' — the earnest self-improvement language colliding with the substance-addicted reality. The specific phrase 'high on crack cocaine' (not just 'crack' but the full clinical term) adds a formal dignity to the desperation. Among the episode's best callbacks.

jokes.text: Their plan to get Frank's money and then 'zip right off to rehab' because 'we're not gonna stop smoking crack'
jokes.setup: Dennis suggests getting Frank's check and using it to go to rehab
jokes.punchline: He adds 'cause we're not gonna stop smoking crack' — framing rehab not as a desire to quit but as the only logical response to a certain-to-continue habit
jokes.explanation: Good dark logic joke — rehab as an admission that you can't stop, not an aspiration to stop. Classic Dennis problem-solving: plan around the worst-case behavior rather than changing it.

jokes.text: Dennis at the welfare office: 'Hi. I'm a recovering crackhead, and this is my donkey-brained sister that I take care of. I'd like some welfare, please.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee go to the welfare office to get money for crack while waiting for Frank's check
jokes.punchline: Dennis introduces himself with 'recovering crackhead' (it's been about 20 minutes since he was smoking crack), introduces Dee as 'donkey-brained,' and requests welfare with a 'please' as if ordering at a restaurant
jokes.explanation: Three jokes packed into two sentences. 'Recovering crackhead' (minutes removed from smoking crack), 'donkey-brained sister I take care of' (describing Dee as a dependent while also insulting her), and the genteel 'I'd like some welfare, please' (treating a welfare application like a service transaction). The politeness is what makes it. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Dee humming while Dennis introduces her as mentally disabled
jokes.setup: Dennis introduces Dee as his 'donkey-brained sister' at the welfare office
jokes.punchline: Dee's response is to simply hum — apparently playing the role, or just vacant from crack withdrawal
jokes.explanation: Physical reaction beat that works visually but doesn't have much content. The ambiguity (is she acting, or is she actually that far gone?) is the slight saving grace.

jokes.text: Welfare officer: 'Well, you clearly replaced the name Frank with the name Dee, and you crossed out the word "not" on this document.'
jokes.setup: Dennis presents fraudulent documentation to prove Dee is mentally disabled
jokes.punchline: The forgery is so obvious — just crossing out 'not' and replacing a name — that the officer calls it out immediately
jokes.explanation: The specific level of incompetence here (crossing out 'not' — the laziest possible forgery) is very funny. The officer's flat delivery of the obvious is a good straight-man beat. The Gang's consistent overestimation of their own schemes meeting reality is a show staple.

jokes.text: Welfare officer, done with the con, just tells them to fill out paperwork — 'I'm done with this bullshit'
jokes.setup: The officer has seen through the scheme; Dennis is about to launch into more justification
jokes.punchline: The officer cuts him off: none of this matters, just fill out the form — the bureaucratic machine doesn't care about the theater
jokes.explanation: Good subversion of the scheme-exposed trope — instead of consequences, they just get what they wanted anyway. The officer's exhaustion ('I'm done with this bullshit') is a good reaction beat. The joke is on the welfare system as much as the Gang.

jokes.text: Dennis and Dee celebrate the welfare process: 'Obama just gives you the money; it's great.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee are relieved they just have to fill out paperwork instead of prove their case
jokes.punchline: Dennis celebrates: 'Obama just gives you the money; it's great' — presenting government assistance as a personal gift from Obama, in a smug, entitled way
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Dennis and Dee are exactly the type of welfare cheats who would dismiss social programs as handouts while also taking them. The 'Obama just gives you the money' framing is a perfect satire of a certain type of entitlement mentality.

jokes.text: Mac bumps into Frank at the welfare office having also failed to keep him away; Frank observes: 'You guys are back on crack, Frank brought strippers back to my place... and yet I'm the only person who thinks it's 2006.'
jokes.setup: Frank surveys the scene: everyone is at the welfare office, Dennis and Dee are on crack again, he apparently brought strippers home — the whole plan has collapsed
jokes.punchline: Frank's summary observation — that all the chaos is happening but he's the only one with an unconventional view of reality — lands as an absurdist truth
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliantly constructed summary joke. Frank's observation is technically the most sane reading of events (everyone is a mess), and his self-designation as the only 'crazy' one is deliciously ironic. It functions as both a plot recap and a meta-comment on the show's premise. Among the episode's best lines. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Frank calls the attorney 'toots' and cackles
jokes.setup: Frank meets a professional female attorney, Lauren Kerwin
jokes.punchline: Frank greets her with 'Hello, toots' and immediately cackles — operating under 2006-era Frank social norms
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe. 'Toots' as a period-appropriate Frank greeting is character-consistent. The cackle is the visual extra. Not exceptional but reliable character comedy.

jokes.text: Frank asks for 'Jer-Bear' (Mr. Doran) — the attorney reveals he's been dead for years
jokes.setup: Frank confidently asks to see 'Jer-Bear' as if picking up a 2006 relationship
jokes.punchline: The attorney reveals Jerry has been dead for years — Frank's 2006 mindset crashes into present-day mortality
jokes.explanation: Good dark beat. Frank's happy anticipation of reuniting with 'Jer-Bear' makes the death announcement land with extra weight. The casualness of 'he's been dead for years, so...' is well-played.

jokes.text: Frank laughing at the death announcement, then calling out 'Jerry! Come on in here' — convinced it's a bit
jokes.setup: The attorney announces Jerry Doran has been dead for years
jokes.punchline: Frank laughs it off, then literally calls out for Jerry to emerge from hiding — convinced his money man has 'made his secretary pull that bit'
jokes.explanation: Frank calling the death announcement 'that bit' is a good character moment — his refusal to accept unwanted information as real mirrors his refusal to accept it's not 2006. Also a nice callback echo to Dennis's 'don't do bits' line.

jokes.text: Frank shows the attorney the phone Dennis claims to have invented; she is unimpressed; Frank erupts: 'You goddamn bitch! You wouldn't know a good idea if it smacked you in a tit!'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee present the 'invention' (a smartphone they clearly didn't invent) to the attorney as evidence of their entrepreneurial future
jokes.punchline: The attorney's clear skepticism triggers Frank's explosive defense of his children's fake inventions — 'smacked you in a tit' as a Frank-specific colorful formulation
jokes.explanation: 'You wouldn't know a good idea if it smacked you in a tit' is a great Frank insult — specific, colorful, delivered in full paternal fury on behalf of a fake invention. The irony of Frank being the one defending the con he doesn't know is a con adds dark comedic texture.

jokes.text: Dennis and Dee try to show the lawyer the iPhone as evidence of their success — silence/reaction beat from the lawyer
jokes.setup: Frank has been building up Dennis and Dee as brilliant iPhone inventors
jokes.punchline: Dennis shows the lawyer his phone, the room falls silent, and then the lawyer clearly fails to be impressed — leading to Frank's explosion
jokes.explanation: The awkward pause after showing the phone to the lawyer (who clearly knows they didn't invent it) is a good cringe beat. The transcript's '[exhales]' stage direction at 16:20 captures the comedic silence. Sets up Frank's explosion well.

jokes.text: Frank: 'She's gonna be gone by 2007, you mark my words!'
jokes.setup: Frank is furious at the attorney's skepticism about Dennis and Dee's phone invention
jokes.punchline: Frank predicts her professional demise 'by 2007' — still operating in 2006, so this is a one-year professional death sentence
jokes.explanation: The 2007 detail does the heavy lifting — it grounds the threat in Frank's temporal confusion and makes what should be a distant prediction sound almost immediate. The 'you mark my words' construction suits Frank's confident bombast.

jokes.text: Dennis and Dee's simultaneous muted echo-insults: 'She's a stupid... stupid idiot.' / 'Yes, she's a dumb... dumb bitch.' / 'A stupid moron.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just unleashed on the attorney; Dennis and Dee trail behind trying to match his energy
jokes.punchline: Their insults are hilariously redundant and unoriginal — 'stupid idiot,' 'dumb bitch,' 'stupid moron' — the deflation from Frank's colorful fury to their generic pile-ons
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the contrast — Frank delivered a genuinely colorful insult, while Dennis and Dee's attempts are embarrassingly generic. Good deflation gag but limited on its own.

jokes.text: Frank pivot on Haiti: 'Haiti's a lost cause. You might as well sink that goddamn island.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee pivot to the Haiti charity as a vehicle for Frank's money; Frank was just charitable-minded moments ago
jokes.punchline: Frank dismisses Haiti entirely: 'lost cause, might as well sink the island' — a 180-degree shift from his stated desire to help the poor
jokes.explanation: 'You might as well sink that goddamn island' is a good dark line delivered with casual indifference. The contrast with Frank's earlier altruistic statements is sharp and reveals how little principles matter to him in practice.

jokes.text: Frank writes Dennis and Dee a large check — 'that's a lot of zeroes' — but it's dated 2006
jokes.setup: Frank announces he wants to help his children and gives them a check
jokes.punchline: The payoff — revealed later at the bank — is that the check is dated 2006 and can't be cashed. The setup is a fake victory.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural payoff for the episode's central premise. The check that can't be cashed because it's dated 2006 is the logical and inevitable consequence of the time-displacement gimmick. The extended buildup (multiple scenes earning the check) makes the collapse funnier. This is the episode's thesis joke.

jokes.text: Mac's formal roommate interview — 'I want to thank you, gentlemen, for your interest in the roommate position. We have Edgar and Trevor, who is an aspiring jazz musician.'
jokes.setup: Mac is conducting a formal interview process for a room in Charlie's squalid apartment
jokes.punchline: The corporate formality of Mac's interview language ('excellent candidates') applied to a hole-in-the-wall apartment is the joke — plus the introduction of 'Edgar' and 'Trevor' as apparently serious candidates
jokes.explanation: Good character-incongruity setup. Mac's formal HR language applied to Charlie's squalor is a solid bit of character comedy. Functions as setup for the roommate interview sequence.

jokes.text: Cat food interview question — Charlie explaining he'd eat the cat food if sleepy
jokes.setup: Mac asks the roommate candidates what they'd do if they found a can of cat food in the apartment
jokes.punchline: Charlie explains he'd eat the cat food not just if hungry but also 'if sleepy' — apparently cat food has soporific properties in his world
jokes.explanation: Charlie eating cat food for sleep as well as hunger is a brilliant detail — it's not just that he eats cat food (established show mythology), but that he's developed a whole pharmacology around it. The 'or sleepy' delivery as a matter-of-fact alternative use is perfect Charlie absurdist logic. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: Mac: 'In what scenario do you not eat the cat food?' Charlie: 'I would always eat the cat food.' Mac: 'Exactly right. See, now there's a man who's thinking on his feet.'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to find a scenario where Charlie wouldn't eat the cat food; Charlie can't conceive of one
jokes.punchline: Mac treats 'I would always eat the cat food' as a correct, impressive answer — giving Charlie points as if this were a legitimate job interview answer
jokes.explanation: Mac awarding points for 'I would always eat the cat food' and calling it thinking-on-your-feet is a great inversion of the interview logic. The question meant to filter out Charlie is now a question only Charlie can pass. Strong absurdist payoff.

jokes.text: Frank reveals he would eat the cat food whether hungry or sleepy — 'I would always eat the cat food' — earning points from Mac
jokes.setup: Frank is asked the same cat food question as the other candidates
jokes.punchline: Frank gives the identical answer to Charlie's answer, confirming the two are spiritually identical — and Mac rewards him
jokes.explanation: Frank mirroring Charlie's answer is a good thematic beat — it reinforces that Frank belongs in this squalor and always has. The parallel construction also shows Mac's interview is functioning as a squalor compatibility test rather than a roommate screen.

jokes.text: Mac calling The Waitress to offer her the room without telling Charlie she'd be living with Charlie
jokes.setup: The Waitress arrives at the interview; Charlie is shocked; Mac reveals he called her
jokes.punchline: Mac: 'I called her... I didn't think you would come if I did [tell you Charlie lived there].' The Waitress: 'You're goddamn right I wouldn't have.'
jokes.explanation: Good use of the Charlie/Waitress dynamic — her categorical refusal to live with Charlie reinforced by the fact that Mac had to deceive her just to get her there. The confirmed mutual dynamic is played for cringe effectively.

jokes.text: Charlie tries to throw The Waitress out the window to 'send her back to 2006' via the time portal
jokes.setup: The Waitress refuses to live with Charlie; Charlie desperately wants to fix the situation
jokes.punchline: Charlie's solution: throw her out the window (the 'time portal') to reset history to 2006 so they can start over
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best physical escalation joke. The time portal theory, introduced as an absurd explanation, is now being applied with literal physical violence — Charlie's solution to romantic rejection is to throw someone through time. The commitment to the bit is what makes it exceptional. The Waitress screaming while Charlie insists 'It's a time portal! Back in time! We could start over again!' is perfect character comedy. High marks across the board.

jokes.text: Frank fully recovered, back to normal — 'What the hell's everybody doing in my apartment? We having a gang bang?'
jokes.setup: Frank appears at the door, apparently snapped back to reality
jokes.punchline: His return to consciousness is signaled by the most Frank possible observation — surveying a room full of people and immediately asking if it's a gang bang
jokes.explanation: Frank's return to baseline is confirmed not by a cogent observation but by an immediate sexual/degenerate assumption. 'We having a gang bang?' is the perfect thesis statement for who Frank Reynolds is. The word 'gang bang' asked as a casual hopeful question captures his entire character in two seconds. Among the episode's most quotable lines.

jokes.text: Frank's memory returning: triggered by Charlie making him a rum ham and Grilled Charlie
jokes.setup: Frank's amnesia began because of the rum ham / Grilled Charlie combo causing him to fall out the window
jokes.punchline: Frank's memories return at the exact moment Charlie makes him another rum ham / Grilled Charlie — the same meal that caused his amnesia is also the cure
jokes.explanation: Elegant structural callback. The rum ham / Grilled Charlie caused the amnesia, and the same meal cures it. The echo of 'rum ham, rum ham' in Frank's recovering memory is well-executed. The fact that Charlie's disgusting food is simultaneously the cause and cure of Frank's brain damage is a perfect Always Sunny joke.

jokes.text: 'Oh, the farts, man. That's good. Oh. Oh, the fart.' — the gang celebrates Frank's return to normalcy via his flatulence
jokes.setup: Frank has returned to his normal self; the gang celebrates
jokes.punchline: The sign of Frank's restoration is that he's farting again — and the gang greets this with warmth and relief
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural callback to the cold open — the episode began with Frank's farting as a problem; it ends with his farting as a celebration and sign of health. The gang's genuine affection for Frank's flatulence as a 'welcome back' signal is both absurd and emotionally resonant in an IASIP way.

jokes.text: End tag: The gang singing Biz Markie's 'Just a Friend' — Charlie replacing lyrics with 'Blah Blah' placeholders
jokes.setup: The episode closes with the gang singing together in apparent contentment despite the failed scheme
jokes.punchline: Charlie, like Dennis earlier with Wyclef, doesn't know the words — substituting 'Blah Blah Blah' for lyrics — but sings with complete commitment
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural callback to Dennis's Wyclef stumble — now Charlie is doing the same thing with Biz Markie. The parallel confirms this is a Gang trait, not just Dennis. The warmth of the ending (they're terrible people who failed spectacularly, singing badly together) is classic IASIP. Charlie's 'Blah Blah Blah' as stand-in lyrics delivered with complete sincerity is very funny.

jokes.text: Final shot: a single trumpet note played off-key, followed by 'Brown.'
jokes.setup: The gang is singing; there's a brief musical interlude
jokes.punchline: A single terrible trumpet note is played, followed by Charlie flatly saying 'Brown.' — no explanation
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — one word, perfectly unexplained. 'Brown.' is the whole joke: an absurdist non-sequitur closing statement that lands because of its total commitment and inexplicability. Very Charlie. The gap between the bad trumpet note and the word 'Brown' is a beautiful awkward silence. A strong closer.

tmdb_overview: Frank falls out the window causing him to think it's 2006, the gang approaches it as a do-over and attempts to fix their past mistakes.
